title: Why People Buy
content: Sales psychology studies why people buy. Core truth: humans decide emotionally and justify rationally. The limbic system (emotion) decides; the neocortex (logic) rationalizes. KEY CONCEPTS: Reach the emotional driver, then arm the buyer with logic. The six core buying emotions: fear, greed, pride, guilt, hope, belonging. WORKED EXAMPLE: A luxury car buyer cites 'safety' (logic) but is driven by status (emotion). PRACTICE: 1) Identify the emotion behind a recent purchase. 2) List the logical reason you told others. 3) Note the gap.

title: The 6 Principles of Influence
content: Cialdini's 6: Reciprocity, Commitment/Consistency, Social Proof, Authority, Liking, Scarcity. KEY CONCEPTS: Reciprocity — give value first. Social proof — 'companies like yours.' Scarcity — legitimate urgency. WORKED EXAMPLE: A free audit (reciprocity) makes prospects feel obligated to hear your pitch. PRACTICE: 1) Design a reciprocity offer. 2) Write a social-proof statement. 3) Create legitimate scarcity for your offer.

title: Loss Aversion & Prospect Theory
content: Kahneman & Tversky: the pain of losing is ~2x the pleasure of gaining. Frame around what the buyer LOSES by not acting. KEY CONCEPTS: Cost of inaction beats potential gains. Anchoring and reference points shape perceived value. WORKED EXAMPLE: 'Every month you wait costs $10K in lost efficiency' outperforms 'you could save $10K.' PRACTICE: 1) Reframe a benefit as a loss avoided. 2) Calculate a prospect's cost of inaction. 3) Set an anchor price.

title: Cognitive Biases in Buying
content: Anchoring, framing, bandwagon, sunk cost, confirmation bias, decoy effect, status quo bias. KEY CONCEPTS: Present the premium option first (anchoring). The decoy effect — a third option makes another look better. Status quo bias (inertia) is your biggest enemy. WORKED EXAMPLE: Three pricing tiers where the middle looks best by design (decoy). PRACTICE: 1) Design a 3-tier offer with a decoy. 2) Identify a bias in your own last purchase. 3) Counter status-quo bias with urgency.

title: Trust & Rapport
content: Trust = (Credibility + Reliability + Intimacy) / Self-Orientation (Maister's Trust Equation). KEY CONCEPTS: Mirroring, active listening, labeling emotions build connection. Vulnerability accelerates trust faster than polish. WORKED EXAMPLE: 'It sounds like you've been burned by vendors before' (labeling) disarms defensiveness. PRACTICE: 1) Score yourself on the Trust Equation. 2) Practice labeling an emotion. 3) Lower your self-orientation in a pitch.

title: Persuasion Psychology in Complex Deals
content: Navigate multiple stakeholders' psychology. Self-persuasion (buyers articulating their own pain) beats being told. KEY CONCEPTS: The Socratic method leads buyers to their own conclusions. Calibrated questions ('How am I supposed to do that?') shift dynamics without confrontation. WORKED EXAMPLE: Instead of arguing price, ask 'What happens if this problem isn't solved this year?' PRACTICE: 1) Write 3 calibrated questions. 2) Design a self-persuasion question sequence.

title: Grandmaster — Ethical Influence Systems
content: Persuasion vs manipulation: ethical persuasion aligns the buyer's genuine interest with your solution (win-win). KEY CONCEPTS: Master sellers would recommend the same choice as the buyer. Build psychologically-informed sales cultures. Design influence into process, not just conversation. WORKED EXAMPLE: A sales system that qualifies OUT bad-fit buyers builds long-term trust and referrals. PRACTICE: 1) Audit a tactic — persuasion or manipulation? 2) Design an ethical qualification gate.

title: King Level — Mastering the Human Mind
content: At King level you understand human decision-making so deeply you shape markets ethically. KEY CONCEPTS: Read individual and collective psychology. Build brands and movements people identify with (Unity — the 7th principle). Create demand by reframing how people see their own problems. WORKED EXAMPLE: A category leader reframes an entire market's self-perception, making its solution feel inevitable. PRACTICE: 1) Define the identity your best customers want. 2) Design a message that reframes their problem. 3) Build unity around a shared mission.
